title: Why git commit -am skips new files
hook: YOU COMMITTED. pay.py NEVER MADE IT.
question: Before commit: git add . or each file by name?
fact_source: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-commit (-a/--all: Automatically stage files that have been modified and deleted, but new files you have not told Git about are not affected) + https://git-scm.com/docs/git-status (?? is used for untracked paths); outputs reproduced with git 2.47.3

scenes.headline: Your new file never got committed
scenes.sub: git commit -am: 1 file changed. pay.py: still untracked.
scenes.voice: You ran git commit dash a m, but your new file never got committed?
scenes.caption: You ran git commit -am, but your new file never got committed?

scenes.headline: -a only stages tracked files
scenes.voice: Dash a only stages files git already tracks. New files you have not told git about are skipped.
scenes.caption: -a only stages files Git already tracks. New files you have not told Git about are skipped.

scenes.headline: git add the new file first
scenes.voice: Run git add pay dot p y first, then commit. Now the commit shows two files changed, not one.
scenes.caption: Run git add pay.py first, then commit. Now the commit shows 2 files changed, not 1.

scenes.headline: Check git status first
scenes.voice: Pro tip: run git status before you commit. Two question marks mean untracked.
scenes.caption: Pro tip: run git status before you commit. ?? means untracked.

scenes.voice: Before you commit, do you run git add dot, or add each file by name? Comment your answer.
scenes.caption: Before you commit, do you run git add . or add each file by name? Comment your answer.

scenes.voice: Follow K four coding for part eight.
scenes.caption: Follow K4Coding for part 8.
